lines.watchItem: Advanced packaging remains the gate on how much accelerator revenue the chain can realize: lines are booked through 2027, NVIDIA has reserved roughly 800,000 to 850,000 wafers of 2026 capacity, and the supply-demand gap is still put at about 20 percent even as monthly output climbs toward 130,000 to 140,000 wafers. Watch whether the gap narrows as the added capacity lands.

Stacked memory, not packaging, is now the tighter limit on shipped units: NVIDIA says it has supply for about 70 percent of demand, guided fiscal 2028 growth to about 70 percent against customer forecasts implying roughly 140 percent, and its memory suppliers can meet only 60 to 70 percent of requested volume for the next top-end part. Packaging slots booked against accelerators that cannot get memory is the exposure to watch.

Leading-edge wafer demand keeps broadening while the layer beneath it tightens: TSMC raised 2026 revenue growth guidance to slightly above 40 percent and capital spending to $60-64 billion, and GlobalWafers reports its 300mm, 200mm and 150mm lines at effectively full utilization with constraints already showing on some advanced 300mm products. Watch whether blank-wafer and memory tightness caps the wafer starts the order book implies.

The leading-node customer base is widening from merchant GPU vendors toward buyers designing their own parts: Microsoft is reported in talks for upward of 300,000 Maia 300 chips for 2027 with a long-term goal above one million units, OpenAI's first inference chip uses a 3nm process with Broadcom, and Marvell's expanded Google agreement carries a warrant implying a cumulative ceiling near $120 billion. Anthropic is separately in early talks with Samsung on a 2nm custom chip.

Packaging demand sits with very few names: the top three customers hold more than 85 percent of capacity with NVIDIA at roughly 60 percent, and NVIDIA's own revenue shows three direct customers at 21, 17 and 16 percent. A single large buyer slowing orders would leave capacity that is hard to refill quickly.

Pricing conditions across the chain are firm: TSMC posted a 67.7 percent gross margin in the second quarter of 2026, up 9.1 points year over year, Samsung raised advanced contract chipmaking prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders in July 2026, and NVIDIA is reported to be raising AI server system prices by more than 15 percent for shipments from early next year. Watch how far memory cost inflation travels into end prices before it meets buyer resistance.

A second packaging route is gaining real orders: Google has committed to more than 3 million units of Intel's embedded bridge packaging for a next-generation in-house chip delivering in 2028, Intel reports high demand and a growing backlog for that bridge packaging targeting high-volume production in 2027, and TSMC responded by announcing a similar bridge technology with Kinsus in late July 2026. Secondary coverage still puts Intel near 13.7 percent of global 2.5D packaging capacity against about 70 percent for TSMC, and Intel's bridge route depends on a single fully booked silicon capacitor supplier.

Policy and buyer financing sit under the order book. Washington is reported to be preparing semiconductor tariffs extending to finished data-center servers, with duty-free allowances sized to each company's US fabrication investment and no rate or start date set; enforcement is widening, with an unproven and unconfirmed investigation into a freight forwarder over 47 Nvidia server shipments, and NVIDIA has cut one customer guarantee from $250 billion to under $120 billion while lining up over $500 billion of third-party capital.
